subject: Quantitative Aptitude
topic: Probability — Coins, Dice, Cards and Combinatorics (W10)

questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed once. What is the probability of getting a tail?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Sample space = {H, T}, each equally likely. P(Tail) = 1/2. Trap: 1/4 assumes two coins; 1/3 is a common misconception treating H, T, and edge as outcomes.

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting a prime number?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Prime numbers on a die (1–6): 2, 3, 5 — that's 3 primes out of 6 outcomes. P(prime) = 3/6 = 1/2. Note: 1 is NOT a prime number. Trap: 1/3 counts only one prime (common if students count 1 as prime, leaving 2 and 3 as the 'small' primes and miscount); 5/6 counts composite + prime incorrectly.

questions.stem: Two fair coins are tossed simultaneously. What is the probability of getting exactly one head?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Sample space = {HH, HT, TH, TT} — 4 outcomes. Exactly one head: {HT, TH} — 2 outcomes. P = 2/4 = 1/2. Trap: 1/4 counts only one of the two favorable outcomes; 3/4 is P(at least one head), not exactly one.

questions.stem: A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. What is the probability of drawing an Ace?
questions.explanation: C is correct. There are 4 Aces in a 52-card pack. P(Ace) = 4/52 = 1/13. Trap: 1/52 (probability of one specific card); 4/26 = 2/13 is wrong (reduces incorrectly). A standard pack has 4 suits × 13 cards = 52 cards total; each denomination (Ace through King) appears 4 times.

questions.stem: Two dice are rolled simultaneously. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers shown is 7?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Total outcomes = 6×6 = 36. Pairs summing to 7: (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1) = 6 pairs. P = 6/36 = 1/6. Sum of 7 is the most likely sum with two dice. Trap: 7/36 is wrong (overcounts); 1/7 mistakenly uses the target sum as denominator.

questions.stem: A bag contains 3 red balls and 4 blue balls. One ball is drawn at random. What is the probability it is red?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Total balls = 3+4 = 7. P(red) = 3/7. Trap: 3/4 uses only the blue ball count as denominator; 4/7 gives P(blue) instead; 1/3 divides by only the red count.

questions.stem: A bag contains 3 red and 4 blue balls. Two balls are drawn one after another WITHOUT replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.explanation: C is correct. P(1st red) = 3/7. After removing one red, P(2nd red | 1st red) = 2/6 = 1/3. P(both red) = (3/7)×(1/3) = 3/21 = 1/7. Alternatively: C(3,2)/C(7,2) = 3/21 = 1/7. Trap: 9/49 = (3/7)² applies WITH replacement; 2/7 makes an arithmetic error in the conditional.

questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed 3 times. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
questions.explanation: C is correct. P(at least one head) = 1 − P(no head) = 1 − P(all tails) = 1 − (1/2)³ = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8. Complementary counting is the fastest approach for 'at least one' problems. Trap: 3/8 = P(exactly one head); 5/8 = P(exactly two or three heads) via wrong counting; 1/8 = P(all tails) — the complement.

questions.stem: Person A speaks the truth 3/4 of the time and person B speaks the truth 4/5 of the time. What is the probability that they contradict each other when asked about an event?
questions.explanation: C is correct. They contradict when one tells truth and other lies. P(A true, B lies) = (3/4)×(1/5) = 3/20. P(A lies, B true) = (1/4)×(4/5) = 4/20. P(contradict) = 3/20 + 4/20 = 7/20. Trap: 12/20 = (3/4)×(4/5) = P(both tell truth, i.e., they agree); 3/20 is only one case.

questions.stem: Two cards are drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that both are Kings?
questions.explanation: B is correct. P = C(4,2)/C(52,2) = 6/1326 = 1/221. C(4,2)=6 (ways to choose 2 kings from 4), C(52,2)=1326 (ways to choose any 2 from 52). Alternatively: (4/52)×(3/51) = 12/2652 = 1/221. Trap: 1/169 = (1/13)² — applies WITH replacement; 4/52 = P(one king in one draw).
